error_modes.label: R/T PROCEDURE KNOWLEDGE AND UNAIDED EXECUTION

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published R/T procedures for the sortie, did not execute the radio procedures without support from the IP, with the result that the content of three or more transmissions had to be dictated from the rear cockpit and the IP took the radios for at least one exchange. The ground and departure calls were produced only after direct prompting, and one required initial call was omitted altogether. Radio handling stayed dependent on IP intervention up to engine shutdown.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published R/T procedures for the sortie, did not execute the radio procedures unaided, with the result that two transmissions were built only after verbal prompting from the IP and each was delayed by more than 10 seconds. SP corrected the format once prompted and no transfer of the radios was necessary. Recall of the sequence of calls remained at the limit of the acceptable standard for the whole sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to incomplete recall of the sequence of calls for the departure phase, did not order the required transmissions correctly on the first attempt, with the result that one call was made out of sequence and was self-corrected within about 5 seconds. SP identified the omission unaided and completed the sequence before the frequency change. No prompting and no intervention by the IP were required.
texts.3: SP executed the R/T procedures for the whole sortie without any support from the IP. All required calls were made at the correct points, in the correct order and with the correct content. SP demonstrated sound knowledge of the proper operation and use of the R/T from engine start to engine shutdown.
texts.4: SP executed every required radio procedure unaided, with no omission and no reordering across the entire sortie. Transmission content was complete and correctly formatted on the first attempt in every phase, including the non-routine exchanges. SP's handling of the equipment showed a precise working knowledge of the operation and use of the R/T.
texts.marginal: SP executed the radio procedures within standards, but recall of the less frequent calls was slower than the routine ones and required a visible pause before each transmission. The trend is toward hesitation whenever the expected sequence of calls changes. SP is expected to consolidate the full sequence by study so that the non-routine transmissions are produced as readily as the routine ones.

error_modes.label: CONTINUOUS MONITORING AND RESPONSE TO CALLS

texts.0: SP, due to attention captured by a minor system indication while the aircraft state went unmonitored, did not continuously monitor the assigned frequency, with the result that two calls addressed to the aircraft went unanswered and the IP replied on SP's behalf. The controller repeated one call three times before any response was made. A traffic advisory that applied to the aircraft was also missed.
texts.1: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single caution indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not respond as soon as possible to a call from the ground station, with the result that the reply was transmitted about 15 seconds after the call and only after the IP pointed out that the aircraft had been addressed. SP then answered correctly with no further prompting. The listening watch was re-established but remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the engine instruments during the climb, did not answer the ground station on the first call, with the result that the reply was delayed by about 5 seconds and was made on SP's own initiative after the call was repeated once. SP restored the listening watch immediately and answered every following call without delay. No IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP monitored the assigned frequency continuously throughout the sortie. Every call addressed to the aircraft was answered on the first transmission and without delay. Calls addressed to other aircraft were monitored and used to maintain the traffic picture.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted listening watch on the assigned frequency in all phases, including the highest-workload segments. Every call was answered immediately and correctly on first transmission, and SP anticipated the traffic situation from the calls addressed to other aircraft. No call to the aircraft was missed or had to be repeated at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the listening watch within standards, but responses were consistently slower during the phases with the highest cockpit workload than at any other time. The trend is toward attention narrowing away from the radio whenever a manual task is in progress. SP is expected to keep the listening watch equally active during the busy segments of the sortie.

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not obtain contact with the ground station following the standard procedures and phraseology, with the result that the initial call had to be repeated three times and the controller requested clarification of the aircraft's intentions. Call sign and position elements were transmitted in the wrong order and one request was misunderstood by the controller. The IP took the radios to re-establish the exchange.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology in constructing the initial call, did not use the prescribed format for contact with the ground station, with the result that two initial calls were incomplete and were rebuilt only after the IP dictated the missing elements. Each call was accepted by the controller on the second transmission. Phraseology remained at the limit of the acceptable standard for the rest of the sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, did not use the prescribed phraseology on one initial contact, with the result that one element was transmitted in the wrong order and was corrected by SP within the same exchange, about 4 seconds later. SP recognized the error without any prompting and re-transmitted in the standard format. The controller required no clarification.
texts.3: SP obtained contact with the ground stations and with other aircraft using the standard procedures and phraseology on every occasion. Call content was complete, correctly ordered and delivered at a rate the controller accepted on first transmission. No call required clarification.
texts.4: SP used standard phraseology precisely on every transmission of the sortie, including the non-routine requests. Initial contacts were complete and correctly formatted on first transmission and were accepted without any request for repetition. Delivery was clear, correctly paced and unambiguous throughout.
texts.marginal: SP used standard phraseology within standards, but delivery was rushed on the longer initial calls and elements were run together. The trend is toward degraded clarity as the length of the transmission increases. SP is expected to pace the transmission so that the standard format stays distinct in the longer calls.

error_modes.label: READ-BACK ACCURACY AND COMPLIANCE WITH INSTRUCTIONS

texts.0: SP, due to a read-back produced from expectation rather than from the instruction as transmitted, did not follow the instructions of the ground station precisely, with the result that an assigned level was read back incorrectly and flown 1000 ft in error until the IP intervened. The controller reissued the instruction twice. SP also accepted and started to act on a clearance addressed to another aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a read-back produced from expectation rather than from the instruction as transmitted, did not reproduce the ground station instruction accurately, with the result that two read-backs contained the wrong frequency and were corrected only after the IP pointed out the discrepancy. No incorrect action was taken on the aircraft. Accuracy in complying with instructions remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a partial note of the clearance taken while hand-flying, did not read back the full instruction on the first attempt, with the result that one element was omitted and was requested and confirmed by SP about 5 seconds later. SP identified the gap unaided and complied correctly with the complete instruction. Neither a controller correction nor an IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP followed the instructions given by the ground stations precisely and without misinterpretation. Every clearance was read back completely and accurately on first transmission and was complied with as issued. No instruction had to be repeated by the controller.
texts.4: SP read back every clearance of the sortie completely and accurately on first transmission and complied with each one exactly as issued. Instructions that changed the planned profile were absorbed and executed without hesitation and without any request for repetition. No misinterpretation occurred at any point of the mission.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the ground station instructions within standards, but the longer clearances were read back only after a pause and from memory alone. The trend is toward incomplete retention as the number of elements in a clearance grows. SP is expected to note the multi-element clearances so that the read-back is delivered complete and without delay.

texts.0: SP, due to transmitting immediately on selecting the new frequency without listening out first, did not avoid interrupting communication between the ground station and other aircraft, with the result that three transmissions were blocked and one clearance issued to another aircraft had to be repeated. The required initial contact on the new frequency was then omitted. The IP took the radios to restore the exchange.
texts.1: SP, due to an inadequate listening period after the frequency change, did not wait for the ongoing exchange to end before keying the microphone, with the result that one transmission was blocked and the initial contact was made about 20 seconds late, after the IP prompted it. SP blocked no further call once prompted. Frequency change discipline remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a short listening period after selecting the new frequency, did not confirm that the frequency was clear before transmitting, with the result that one call overlapped the end of another aircraft's transmission and SP released the transmit switch and re-transmitted within about 3 seconds. The initial contact was then completed correctly and unprompted. No transmission had to be repeated by the controller.
texts.3: SP listened out on each new frequency before transmitting and interrupted no exchange between the ground station and other aircraft. The required initial contact was executed on every frequency change, at the correct time and with the correct content. No transmission was blocked during the sortie.
texts.4: SP managed every frequency change cleanly, listening out first and selecting a gap in the traffic for each initial contact. No transmission of any other station was blocked at any point in the sortie, and each required initial call followed the change promptly. Frequency selection and the associated calls were fully integrated with the phase of flight.
texts.marginal: SP observed frequency change discipline within standards, but on the busier frequencies the pause before the initial call was shorter than the traffic volume warranted. The trend is toward keying the microphone before the frequency picture is complete. SP is expected to establish the traffic situation on the new frequency before every initial contact.

error_modes.label: INTEGRATION OF R/T WITH AIRCRAFT CONTROL AND WORKLOAD

texts.0: SP, due to workload distribution that left the SP flying and transmitting at the same time, did not establish two-way communication with the ground station at the required point, with the result that the departure call was made about two minutes late and the aircraft departed the briefed profile while the call was being built. Aircraft control was handed to the IP so that the transmission could be completed. Two later calls were made by the IP.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to shed a secondary task when workload increased, did not keep the radio work separated from the flying task, with the result that a required call was delayed by about 30 seconds and was transmitted only after the IP directed that it be made. Flight parameters were held while the call was built, but no further radio work was attempted until the workload reduced. Task management on the radio remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the radio work inside the turn, did not transmit at the planned point in the pattern, with the result that the call was made about 10 seconds late once the aircraft was established on the new heading. SP recognized the conflict between the two tasks and deferred the transmission without any prompting. The remaining calls were re-sequenced correctly against the flying task.
texts.3: SP integrated the radio work with the flying task throughout the sortie. Two-way communication was established with each ground station and with other aircraft at the required points, with no degradation of the flight parameters. Transmissions were timed to fit the phase of flight.
texts.4: SP handled the R/T and the aircraft together with no measurable cost to either. Every required contact was established at the planned point and the flight parameters were held precisely while transmitting, including in the highest-workload phases. Radio work was sequenced ahead of the aircraft rather than in reaction to it.
texts.marginal: SP combined the radio work with the flying task within standards, but transmissions during the manoeuvring segments came at the expense of a visible pause in the scan. The trend is toward serialising the two tasks instead of interleaving them. SP is expected to plan the timing of the calls so that the flying task carries no pause when the microphone is keyed.

error_modes.label: BREVITY AND UNREQUIRED VERBIAGE ON THE FREQUENCY

texts.0: SP, due to adding verbiage that is not required to nearly every transmission, did not keep the calls to the information the controller needed in the format expected, with the result that meaningless phrases such as 'with you' and 'be advised' extended six calls on a congested frequency and two of them were cut off by the controller. Airtime lost to the padding delayed the clearance to another aircraft. The IP took the radios and rebuilt the outstanding requests in the standard format.
texts.1: SP, due to adding verbiage that is not required to the routine calls, did not keep the transmissions to the information needed and nothing more, with the result that four calls carried meaningless phrases and the padding was dropped only after the IP directed it twice. Call content was correct once the extra wording was removed and no transmission had to be repeated by the controller. Brevity remained at the limit of the acceptable standard for the rest of the sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to habitual use of 'checking in' when establishing on a new frequency, did not open the exchange with the information needed and nothing more, with the result that the first two calls carried unrequired verbiage before SP dropped the phrase unaided. The remaining initial calls were transmitted in the standard format. No prompting from the IP was required and no airtime was lost on the busier frequencies.
texts.3: SP transmitted only the information the controllers needed, nothing more and nothing less, in the format expected. No call carried meaningless phrases such as 'with you', 'at this time' or 'be advised'. Frequency airtime was used efficiently in every phase of the sortie.
texts.4: SP kept every transmission to the minimum content that carried the message, with no unrequired verbiage in any call including the non-routine requests. Even on the most congested frequency each call was tight enough to be accepted by the controller on first transmission. Brevity was achieved without the loss of any required element.
texts.marginal: SP kept the transmissions brief within standards, but on the busier frequencies a filler phrase reappeared at the start of the longer requests. The trend is toward padding whenever the call takes more than a few seconds to build. SP is expected to compose the request before keying the microphone so that no filler is needed.

error_modes.label: COMPLETENESS OF REQUESTS AND CONTROLLER QUERIES

texts.0: SP, due to omitting information the controller needed from the request, did not provide the elements in the format expected, with the result that four transmissions were followed by a controller query for the missing position or intention and one request was denied for lack of detail. Three repeat exchanges consumed airtime on a busy frequency. The IP took the radios to complete the request.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting needed information from the requests, did not give the controller the elements expected on the first transmission, with the result that two requests were completed only after a controller query and the missing element was supplied by the IP from the rear cockpit. No request was denied and each exchange was closed on the second transmission. Completeness of the calls remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to omitting the location element from the request for return to base, did not give the controller the information needed on the first transmission, with the result that one query was generated and SP supplied the area and altitude within about 5 seconds. SP recognized the omission before the controller had finished the query. The later requests carried agency, call sign, location and request without prompting.
texts.3: SP provided the controllers with the information needed on every request, nothing missing and nothing surplus. No transmission generated a query for information that should have been included. Each exchange was closed on the first transmission.
texts.4: SP built every request complete on the first transmission, including the non-routine ones, so that no controller query for missing information was generated at any point in the sortie. Location, intention and any restriction were carried in the call as required. The exchanges consumed the minimum airtime the traffic allowed.
texts.marginal: SP supplied complete requests within standards, but on the non-routine calls one element was recovered only after a pause inside the transmission. The trend is toward assembling the content while transmitting rather than before. SP is expected to fix all four elements of the call before keying so that no controller query is invited.

error_modes.label: ATTENTION-GETTING CALL BEFORE A DETAILED REQUEST

texts.0: SP, due to making a long detailed request without first getting the controller's attention, did not split the exchange into an attention call and the request that follows the acknowledgement, with the result that the full request was repeated three times on a congested frequency and the controller twice replied that the transmission had not been received. Confusion over which aircraft was requesting delayed the clearance by about two minutes. The IP took the radios and re-established the exchange in two steps.
texts.1: SP, due to transmitting the full detail before the controller had acknowledged the call sign, did not get the controller's attention first, with the result that two long requests had to be repeated in full and the two-step format was adopted only after the IP directed it. Both requests were then accepted on the first attempt. Handling of the detailed requests remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the detail in the same transmission as the initial call, did not wait for the controller to acknowledge before stating the request, with the result that the first request was repeated once and SP reverted to the two-step format unaided within about 10 seconds. No prompting from the IP was required. Every later detailed request was passed in two steps.
texts.3: SP obtained the controller's attention with a short call giving the agency and call sign, then stated the request after the acknowledgement. Every detailed request was passed in two steps and was accepted on the first attempt. No request generated confusion or a repetition on the frequency.
texts.4: SP separated the attention call from the detail on every non-routine request, including a multi-part request on a congested frequency, and no exchange required a repetition. The detail was stated only after the acknowledgement and at a rate the controller took on the first pass. Frequency congestion was not increased by any transmission SP made.
texts.marginal: SP used the two-step format within standards, but the detail occasionally began before the controller's acknowledgement was complete. The trend is toward compressing the two steps into one whenever the frequency sounds quiet. SP is expected to hold the detail until the acknowledgement has finished on every detailed request.

error_modes.label: TRANSMISSION TIMING AGAINST OTHER AIRCRAFT AND CRITICAL PHASES

texts.0: SP, due to keying the microphone while another aircraft was in a critical phase of flight, did not anticipate the replies to the controller's transmissions, with the result that an aircraft in the flare was transmitted over and a read-back from a third aircraft was blocked twice. The controller directed all stations to stand by. The IP took the radios for the following exchanges.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to anticipate the other party's reply to the controller, did not withhold the transmission until the exchange had closed, with the result that one call was keyed across an aircraft on short final and SP transmitted again only after the IP directed that the exchange be allowed to finish. No clearance had to be reissued. Transmission timing remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to treating the pause after the controller's instruction as the end of the exchange, did not allow for the read-back that was still to come, with the result that one transmission overlapped the start of another aircraft's read-back and the microphone was released within about 2 seconds. SP then waited for the exchange to close before transmitting again. No further overlap occurred in the sortie.
texts.3: SP timed every transmission so that no other aircraft was transmitted over. Calls were withheld while another aircraft was in a critical phase of flight and while a reply to the controller was still outstanding. No exchange on the frequency was interrupted by SP.
texts.4: SP anticipated the reply to every controller transmission and used only the gaps that remained, so that no aircraft was blocked at any point in the sortie. Calls were deliberately withheld while other aircraft were in the flare or on short final. The timing of the transmissions matched the traffic picture throughout.
texts.marginal: SP timed the transmissions within standards, but the interval left after another aircraft's call was shorter whenever SP had a request pending. The trend is toward keying as soon as the frequency sounds clear rather than after the exchange has closed. SP is expected to allow for the reply that follows every instruction before transmitting.

error_modes.label: PF AND PNF RESPONSIBILITY FOR RADIO CALLS

texts.0: SP, due to transmitting as pilot not flying without notifying the pilot flying, did not observe the division of radio responsibility, with the result that three exchanges were completed unannounced and one of them accepted a runway change the pilot flying was unaware of. The aircraft continued toward the original runway until the IP queried the exchange and intervened. Two calls that belonged to the pilot flying were left for the IP to make.
texts.1: SP, due to transmitting as pilot not flying without first notifying the pilot flying, did not keep the other cockpit informed of what had been passed, with the result that two exchanges went unannounced and were reconstructed only after the IP asked what had been agreed. No clearance that conflicted with the briefed profile was accepted. Coordination of the radio work remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to answering a call as pilot not flying before announcing the intention, did not notify the pilot flying prior to the transmission, with the result that one short exchange went unannounced and SP passed the content across within about 5 seconds of releasing the microphone. Aircraft control was not transferred at any point. Every later transmission was announced before it was made.
texts.3: SP kept the radio calls with the pilot flying and, when transmitting as pilot not flying, notified the pilot flying beforehand and passed the content afterwards. No transmission was made without the other cockpit knowing. Aircraft control was never transferred for the sake of a radio call.
texts.4: SP applied the pilot flying and pilot not flying division of the radio work precisely for the whole sortie, notifying the other cockpit before every transmission made as pilot not flying and confirming the content immediately afterwards. No call was left unaccounted for between the two cockpits. No transfer of aircraft control was needed for any transmission.
texts.marginal: SP observed the division of radio responsibility within standards, but on the shorter replies the notification to the pilot flying came after the microphone had been keyed. The trend is toward announcing the transmission only once it is already under way. SP is expected to notify the pilot flying before keying, whatever the length of the call.

error_modes.label: CLARIFICATION OF UNCERTAIN PHRASEOLOGY IN PLAIN LANGUAGE

texts.0: SP, due to acknowledging a standard phrase whose meaning was not understood instead of clarifying it in plain language, did not establish what had been required before acting, with the result that a conditional instruction was flown as an unconditional one and the aircraft left the assigned area before the IP intervened. The controller reissued the instruction and queried the aircraft's intentions. Two further phrases were acknowledged without comprehension in the same exchange.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to ask the controller for clarification of an unfamiliar standard phrase, did not use plain language to establish its meaning, with the result that the exchange stalled for about 20 seconds and the meaning was supplied by the IP rather than requested from the controller. No incorrect action was taken on the aircraft. Handling of the unfamiliar phraseology remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation over an unfamiliar term in a traffic advisory, did not query it as soon as the doubt arose, with the result that the acknowledgement was delayed by about 10 seconds before SP requested clarification in plain language unaided. The controller restated the advisory and SP complied correctly. No further phrase was left unresolved.
texts.3: SP acted only on instructions whose meaning was clear. Where a standard phrase was not certain, SP requested clarification from the controller in plain language and confirmed the meaning before complying. No instruction was acted on from assumption.
texts.4: SP resolved every uncertainty over the controllers' phraseology at the moment it arose, using plain language that closed the point in a single exchange. No instruction was acknowledged before its meaning had been established and no phrase had to be queried twice. Comprehension was verified without adding avoidable airtime to the frequency.
texts.marginal: SP verified the meaning of the controllers' instructions within standards, but on one non-routine phrase the clarification was requested only after a long pause. The trend is toward waiting to see whether the meaning becomes clear rather than asking for it. SP is expected to ask in plain language as soon as a phrase is in doubt.

error_modes.label: TAXI INSTRUCTIONS ON THE ASSIGNED GROUND CHANNEL

texts.0: SP, due to not listening carefully to the taxi instructions passed on Ch-2, did not take in the routing as it was transmitted, with the result that the instruction had to be requested from the controller twice and one hold short element was missed altogether. The aircraft was turned toward the wrong taxiway before the IP intervened. The IP took the radios for the remainder of the ground phase.
texts.1: SP, due to a divided listening watch while the taxi instructions were being passed on Ch-2, did not take in the full routing as transmitted, with the result that one element had to be requested from the controller again after the IP pointed out that the instruction had not been captured. The aircraft was not moved until the routing was complete. Handling of the ground frequency remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to selecting Ch-2 after the cockpit checks rather than before requesting taxi, did not have the ground frequency established when the instructions were expected, with the result that the request was made about 15 seconds later than planned and SP corrected the channel selection unaided. The instructions were then taken complete on the first transmission. No prompting from the IP was required.
texts.3: SP contacted the ground station on Ch-2 for the taxi instructions and listened carefully to the transmission. The routing was taken complete on the first pass and no element had to be requested again. The exchange on the ground frequency was closed without repetition.
texts.4: SP had Ch-2 selected and the listening watch established before the taxi request was made, and took the complete routing from a single transmission including the conditional elements. No part of the instruction was requested again and none was queried by the controller. The ground exchange consumed the minimum airtime.
texts.marginal: SP handled the taxi instructions within standards, but attention shifted to the cockpit checks while the routing was still being transmitted. The trend is toward listening only to the first elements of a long ground instruction. SP is expected to hold the cockpit tasks until the taxi instruction has been passed in full.
